blaster-master-1988: Sunsoft's Blaster Master (1988) switches between side-view tank runs and overhead caverns, with Jason riding the frog vehicle SOPHIA in the US story. Japan sold the same cartridge as Metafight, with a different science-fiction plot.
dragons-lair: Don Bluth animated Dragon's Lair, the 1983 laserdisc cabinet in which Dirk the Daring's path is chosen rather than freely controlled. The NES cartridge that reuses the name is a conventional action game, not that arcade film.
dragonstrike: SSI's DragonStrike, from 1990, is an Advanced Dungeons & Dragons game about fighting from dragonback. It began on computers; the NES edition is a smaller adaptation of that aerial design.
the-simpsons-bart-vs-the-space-mutants: Acclaim's first licensed Simpsons cartridge, The Simpsons: Bart vs. the Space Mutants, has Bart disguise purple objects so aliens cannot harvest them. It reached the NES in 1991, before the later Bart games.
spider-man-return-of-the-sinister-six: LJN's Spider-Man: Return of the Sinister Six is a side-scrolling NES take on Marvel's villain team. The 1992 cartridge is its own comic license, separate from the 16-bit Spider-Man brawlers.
xevious: Namco's Xevious, a 1982 arcade shooter, makes the Solvalou bomb ground targets and fire at aircraft at the same time. A Famicom port followed; the game's identity is that coin-op, not a much later reissue.
gunsmoke: Capcom's Gun.Smoke is a 1985 Western shooter in which a lone gunman walks up the screen and fires in several directions. An NES conversion later kept the same cowboy premise.
dragon-quest-ii-1987: Enix's Dragon Quest II (1987) follows the prince of Midenhall and his two cousins, with Akira Toriyama's art and Koichi Sugiyama's score. North America later received it as Dragon Warrior II.
sky-destroyer: Taito published Sky Destroyer in 1985 as a rail shooter seen from behind a World War II fighter. The Famicom release, also issued as an arcade game, was not a Western NES original.
top-gunnes: Konami's Top Gun (1987) turns the Tom Cruise film into an NES jet game whose carrier landings became notorious. Miss the approach and the mission fails, however the dogfights went.
nintendo-world-cup: Technos built Nintendo World Cup as a Kunio-kun soccer game, and Nintendo published the foul-heavy Western version in 1990. The Japanese name ties it to the Nekketsu high-school series.
micro-mages: Morphcat Games released Micro Mages in 2019 as a new NES platformer for the original hardware, not a remake. Up to four wizards share one screen, a rare trick on that console.
batman-return-of-the-joker: Sunsoft's Batman: Return of the Joker is a 1991 NES sequel to the studio's earlier Batman cartridge, not a tie-in to the film Batman Returns. It keeps Sunsoft's fast, demanding action.
home-alone: Bethesda Softworks developed the NES Home Alone for THQ, a 1991 license in which Kevin sets traps for the burglars. The Super Nintendo release is a separate production from another team.
marble-madness: Mark Cerny designed Marble Madness for Atari Games, a 1984 trackball race that rolls a marble through isometric courses. Home versions, including an NES port, followed the arcade cabinet.
california-games: Epyx's California Games gathers beach and street events such as surfing, half-pipe skating, and BMX. The 1987 computer sports collection later received an NES port.
antarctic-adventure: Konami's Antarctic Adventure, from 1983, slides the penguin Penta across ice floes toward the South Pole. The Famicom cart is a home version of that arcade trip, not a later original.
soccer: Nintendo's black-box Soccer is the simple overhead Famicom match from 1985, sold beside the company's early baseball and tennis carts. It is that NES sports game, not a Konami or EA title.
side-pocket-1986: Data East's Side Pocket (1986) is pocket billiards, with nine-ball sets plus a trick-shot challenge. Arcade cabinets came first; the NES and later 16-bit versions kept the same table.
dragon-quest-iii-1988: Enix shipped Dragon Quest III (1988) on a Wednesday in Japan so students would not skip school for the RPG. A class-changing hero and Toriyama's monsters made it the Famicom peak of the series.
robocop: Data East's RoboCop puts the film cyborg in a side-scrolling arcade game, with an NES cartridge afterward. Ocean's computer versions are a separate set of licenses, not this coin-op.
bomberman-ii: Hudson Soft's Bomberman II, from 1991, adds new maze stages to the NES bomb-and-brick series. It stays a single-screen blaster, unlike the later Super Bomberman party line.
qbert: Gottlieb's Q*bert hops a pyramid of cubes and flips their colors while snakes and balls intrude. The 1982 arcade character later appeared on the NES, long after the coin-op made him famous.
defender-of-the-crown: Cinemaware's Defender of the Crown is a 1986 Amiga strategy game of Robin Hood-era jousts, raids, and territory. The NES port is a reduced take on that computer original.
mighty-final-fight: Capcom's Mighty Final Fight shrinks Metro City's brawler into a super-deformed NES spinoff in 1993. It is neither the arcade Final Fight nor the Super Nintendo sequels.
strider-1989: Capcom's arcade Strider (1989) sends Hiryu up a futuristic mountain with a climbing tonfa. The NES cart ports that coin-op, while the Genesis Strider is a different and much longer game.
the-immortal: Electronic Arts published The Immortal in 1990, an isometric dungeon adventure that started on the Apple IIGS. The NES edition is a later port of that computer quest.
shadow-of-the-ninja-1990: Natsume's Shadow of the Ninja (1990) puts two ninjas against a future emperor on the NES. European boxes retitle the same cartridge Blue Shadow.
rushn-attack-1985: Konami's Rush'n Attack (1985) is the Western name for the arcade knife-combat game Green Beret. Soldiers cross a military base on foot; an NES port followed the coin-op.
elite: David Braben and Ian Bell created Elite in 1984 on the BBC Micro, an open trading game of wireframe ships and wanted ratings. A Famicom edition came later; it did not begin on Nintendo hardware.
guerrilla-war-1987: SNK's Guerrilla War (1987) is a top-down shooter whose Japanese release, Guevara, names Che Guevara and Fidel as the pair you control. The Western version keeps the shooting and drops those names.
ultima-iii-exodus: Richard Garriott's Ultima III: Exodus, from Origin in 1983, is the party-based chapter that mixes fantasy races on one team. Pony Canyon and FCI later brought a licensed version to the NES.
shinobi-1988: Sega's arcade Shinobi arrived in 1987 with Joe Musashi rescuing kidnapped children. The home cartridge titled Shinobi (1988) is a port, not the coin-op's first appearance.
alien-3: ALIEN³ names several different licensed games spun from the 1993 film, published by LJN. The Genesis version earned the stronger reputation; the Super Nintendo one is a separate design.
dragon-quest-iv: Chapter structure introduces other heroes before the main quest in DRAGON QUEST IV, Enix's 1990 Famicom RPG. Horii, Toriyama, and Sugiyama led it again, and the US name was Dragon Warrior IV.
home-alone-2: Home Alone 2 follows the sequel film, moving Kevin from the first movie's house to a big-city hotel and toy store. NES and Super Nintendo carts are separate early-1990s licenses, not one shared game.
kung-fu-master: Irem's Kung-Fu Master, a 1984 arcade climber called Spartan X in Japan, fights up a building in the manner of a Hong Kong action film. Nintendo's NES release retitles that coin-op Kung Fu.
tom-jerry-the-ultimate-game-of-cat-and-m: Tom & Jerry: The Ultimate Game of Cat and Mouse! is an NES chase based on the MGM cartoon, from around 1991. Jerry crosses side-view stages while Tom tries to catch him.
little-nemo-the-dream-master: Capcom's Little Nemo: The Dream Master, from 1990, adapts the Slumberland film and comic to the NES. Nemo feeds candy to sleeping animals so he can ride them through dream stages.
worms: Team17's Worms, shaped by Andy Davidson and released in 1995, turns artillery duels into cartoon worms on a landscape you can blow apart. It started on the Amiga before Nintendo machines got ports.
wolfenstein-3d: id Software's Wolfenstein 3D, from 1992, sends B.J. Blazkowicz through a Nazi castle and helped popularize PC first-person shooting. The Super Nintendo port censors much of the original imagery.
mortal-kombat: Midway's Mortal Kombat used digitized actors and graphic finishing moves when it reached arcades in 1992. On the Super Nintendo the blood became sweat, a change that fed the violence debate.
doom-2: id Software released DOOM on PC in 1993, and the shareware episode spread far beyond store shelves. Super Nintendo and later Game Boy Advance versions are reduced conversions, not the debut.
eye-of-the-beholder: Westwood developed Eye of the Beholder for SSI, a first-person AD&D crawl under Waterdeep. The computer game is the original; a Super Nintendo port came afterward.
final-fantasy-v: Square's FINAL FANTASY V restores a job system on the Super Famicom in 1992, so characters can change classes. No official English edition existed until long after the Japanese release.
earthworm-jim: Shiny Entertainment and David Perry launched Earthworm Jim in 1994 on the Sega Genesis, a cartoon run-and-gun about a worm in a robotic suit. Super Nintendo and handheld versions followed that Genesis original.
another-world: Eric Chahi's Another World, published by Delphine in 1991, strands a physicist on an alien planet with rotoscoped scenes and almost no text. North America called it Out of This World.
disneys-aladdin-1993: Virgin Interactive's Disney's Aladdin is the 1993 Genesis platformer known for hand-drawn animation of the film's cast. Capcom's Super Nintendo Aladdin is a different game, and the NES and Game Boy editions differ again.
ultimate-mortal-kombat-3: Midway's Ultimate Mortal Kombat 3 revises the arcade Mortal Kombat 3 roster with extra fighters and stages. The 1995 cabinet, and the Super Nintendo port after it, sit one update beyond the first MK3.
prince-of-persia-nes: Jordan Mechner rotoscoped his brother for Prince of Persia (1989), Broderbund's timed Apple II dungeon of traps and sword fights. NES, Super Nintendo, and Game Boy ports came after that computer original.
tetris-1984: Alexey Pajitnov designed Tetris (1984) in Moscow, stacking falling tetrominoes into complete lines. Nintendo's Game Boy edition is a later licensed hit, not this first version.
earthworm-jim-2: Shiny's Earthworm Jim 2 continues the cartoon levels in 1995, including a stage where a puppy must be bounced to safety. Sega hardware led again, with Nintendo ports following.
mortal-kombat-3: Midway's Mortal Kombat 3 adds a run button and cybernetic ninjas to the 1995 arcade lineup. Home editions, including the Super Nintendo one, followed that cabinet.
mortal-kombat-2: Midway's Mortal Kombat 2 widened the roster, and the 1993 Super Nintendo port could restore the blood behind a code. That was a reversal of the first SNES Mortal Kombat's sweat substitute.
the-lion-king: Virgin's Disney's The Lion King turns the 1994 film into a difficult platformer, from the wildebeest gorge onward through Simba's life. Genesis and Super Nintendo copies led the release.
battletoads-double-dragon: Rare's Battletoads & Double Dragon is the 1993 crossover published by Tradewest. NES, Super Nintendo, and Game Boy editions all exist, and they are not the same build.
the-chaos-engine: The Bitmap Brothers' The Chaos Engine is a moody 1993 Amiga shooter sold in the US as Soldiers of Fortune. Two mercenaries fight through a Victorian science-fiction world; a Super Nintendo port exists.
super-3-d-noahs-ark: Wisdom Tree's Super 3-D Noah's Ark is the unlicensed 1994 Super Nintendo game that uses a Wolfenstein-style engine to shoot food at animals. The cart bypassed Nintendo's lockout chip.
rock-n-roll-racing: Silicon & Synapse, later known as Blizzard, made Rock n' Roll Racing for Interplay in 1993. Isometric cars fight while licensed rock songs play between events.
lemmings: DMA Design's Lemmings, published by Psygnosis in 1991, assigns jobs to a marching crowd so the creatures do not walk off cliffs. The Amiga original is the famous one; Nintendo ports came later.
final-fantasy-iv-1991: Square's Final Fantasy IV (1991) introduced the Active Time Battle system and was retitled Final Fantasy II in North America. Cecil's Super Famicom story is the real fourth game, not a sequel to the US numbering.
super-star-wars: LucasArts and Sculptured Software's Super Star Wars adapts A New Hope as a 1992 Super Nintendo action game, Mode 7 races included. It opened a trilogy of film tie-ins on that console.
simcity-2000: Maxis followed its city builder with SimCity 2000 in 1993, switching to an isometric view, underground layers, and a newspaper. A Super Nintendo port came after the PC original.
theme-park: Bullfrog's Theme Park, associated with Peter Molyneux, lets you lay out rides, set prices, and watch guests wander. The 1994 computer management game later received a Super Nintendo port.
darkwing-duck: Capcom's Disney's Darkwing Duck continues the studio's NES Disney platformers in 1992, starring the cartoon duck who poses as a superhero. A Game Boy version was released as well.
final-fantasy-ii-1988: Square's Final Fantasy II (1988) grows statistics through the actions characters take, without the usual experience levels. It is the real second game; the American Super Nintendo Final Fantasy II is actually IV.
super-contra-1988: Konami's arcade Super Contra (1988) is the run-and-gun sequel with both overhead and side-view stages. The NES game Super C is a later, rearranged home edition, not this cabinet.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-ii-the-arca: Konami's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Arcade Game is the 1990 NES port of the studio's coin-op beat 'em up. Two players fight the Foot through the arcade's stages.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-tournament-: Konami's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Tournament Fighters is a one-on-one fighter, and the 1993 NES and Super Nintendo cartridges are different games. Neither continues the earlier side-scrolling brawlers.
mega-man-3-1990: Capcom's Mega Man 3 (1990) introduces the dog Rush and gives Proto Man a role in the story. New support gear sets this NES chapter apart from the first two.
track-field: Konami's Track & Field, called Hyper Olympic in Japan, is a 1983 arcade button-masher of Olympic events. Home versions, the NES one included, kept that rapid tapping.
double-dragon-ii: Technos' Double Dragon II: The Revenge continues Billy and Jimmy Lee, first in arcades in 1988. The NES edition rebuilds the revenge plot with its own stages and moves.
paperboy: Atari Games' Paperboy, from 1985, delivers papers along a suburban street while dodging dogs, skateboards, and broken windows. The cabinet's handlebars are part of its identity; the NES port has none.
adventure-island-1986: Hudson's Adventure Island (1986) is the Famicom game based on Sega's Wonder Boy, starring Master Higgins. The skateboard and thrown axes come from that licensed arcade design.
tiny-toon-adventures: Konami's Tiny Toon Adventures on the NES, from 1991, follows Buster Bunny and the other Acme Acres kids. It is a different cartridge from the later Super Nintendo Buster game.
circus-charlie: Konami's Circus Charlie, a 1984 arcade act, walks a clown through fire hoops, tightropes, and ball balancing. The Famicom port is a home version of that coin-op.
castlevania-ii-simons-quest-1987: Konami's Castlevania II: Simon's Quest (1987) opens the whip sequel into a countryside search with a day-night cycle. Towns and clues replace a straight march through castle stages.
joust: Williams' Joust, from 1982, mounts knights on flying ostriches and rewards the rider who strikes from above. The arcade cabinet is the original; an NES port arrived years later.
mega-man-4: Capcom's Mega Man 4 (1991) adds a chargeable arm cannon and sends the hero against Dr. Cossack before the usual Wily twist. It is still a side-view NES robot run.
batman-the-video-game: Sunsoft's Batman: The Video Game borrows the 1989 film's look but builds original NES stages instead of retelling the movie. Wall jumps and a grappling line define how Batman moves.
lode-runner: Hudson brought Broderbund's gold-digging puzzle to the Famicom, and the US NES edition of Lode Runner followed in 1987. You still dig brick, trap guards, and clear every piece of gold.
galaxian: Namco's Galaxian, from 1979, peels aliens out of formation so they dive at the player, a step past rigid rows. The NES release is a much later port of that arcade shooter.
ducktales-2: Capcom's Disney's DuckTales 2 sends Scrooge McDuck on another NES treasure hunt in 1993, pogo cane included. It is a sequel to the studio's first DuckTales cartridge, not a remake.
wild-gunman-1984: Nintendo's Wild Gunman (1984) is a Famicom light-gun game: outlaws draw, and you fire with the Zapper. An earlier Nintendo electromechanical arcade of the same name dates to the 1970s.
felix-the-cat: Hudson Soft's Felix the Cat turns the classic cartoon into NES and Game Boy platformers in the early 1990s. Felix's bag of tricks carries him through stages; this is not an Adventure Island spinoff.
mega-man-5: Capcom's Mega Man 5 (1992) pits the hero against Gravity Man and Gyro Man, with a charge shot alongside the usual special weapons. Proto Man's apparent betrayal is the NES story hook.
space-invaders-1978: Taito's Space Invaders (1978), designed by Tomohiro Nishikado, marches aliens down the screen and helped make arcade games a mass business. The NES cart is one of many later ports.
contra-force: Konami's Contra Force is a 1992 NES spinoff with no arcade original, starring a task force instead of the usual pair. You can switch members during the run-and-gun stages.
pool-of-radiance: SSI's Pool of Radiance, from 1988, is the first Gold Box AD&D game, set in the Forgotten Realms city of Phlan. The NES version adapts that computer RPG's party combat.
yie-ar-kung-fu-1985: Konami's Yie Ar Kung-Fu (1985) is an early arcade fighter in which Oolong faces opponents who each bring a weapon. The NES edition is a home port of those one-on-one bouts.
balloon-fight-1985: Nintendo's Balloon Fight (1985) owes an obvious debt to Joust: flap, pop rival balloons, and stay out of the water. Balloon Trip mode drops the enemies for a scrolling course of sparks.
donkey-kong-jr: Nintendo's Donkey Kong Jr. reverses the first arcade game: Mario is the captor, and Junior climbs vines to free his father. The 1982 coin-op later received a real NES port.
road-fighter: Konami's Road Fighter is a 1984 overhead arcade racer in which running out of fuel ends the drive. The Famicom version is a port of that coin-op, not a later console-born racing series.
jurassic-park: The name Jurassic Park covers different licensed games for the 1993 film, not one shared design. Ocean's Super Nintendo cart is mostly overhead exploration, while the NES game is a side-scroller.
galaga-1981: Namco's Galaga (1981) follows Galaxian with a tractor beam that can capture your ship so a rescued second fighter doubles your fire. The NES version is a later port of that arcade shooter.
ghosts-n-goblins-1985: Capcom's Ghosts 'n Goblins (1985) strips Arthur to his underwear after one hit in a graveyard of monsters. Both the arcade cabinet and the fierce NES port expect the quest to be beaten twice.
mega-man-6: Capcom's Mega Man 6 (1993) closes the original NES run and adds Rush adapters that fuse with the hero. A figure called Mr. X stands in for the usual villain until late in the game.
lode-runner-1983: Doug Smith wrote Lode Runner (1983), and Broderbund's computer release made the gold-collecting puzzle a hit. Guards chase you through diggable brick; the design predates any Nintendo port.
bubble-bobble-1986: Taito's Bubble Bobble (1986), directed by Fukio Mitsuji, has Bub and Bob trap foes in bubbles they can burst. The NES port keeps the two-dinosaur rescue of their kidnapped girlfriends.
mother: Shigesato Itoi's Mother is the 1989 Famicom RPG later released in English as Earthbound Beginnings. A planned NES localization was cancelled, so that official English name arrived decades later.
ultima-v-warriors-of-destiny: Richard Garriott's Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny, from Origin in 1988, sets the Avatar against Lord British's usurper, Blackthorn. The NES port carries that computer RPG's virtue-based world forward.
golf-1980: Nintendo's Famicom Golf, designed with Shigeru Miyamoto and programmed by Satoru Iwata at HAL, is the stroke-play game later on the NES. The parenthetical year in Golf (1980) is not that cartridge's release.
super-c: North America retitled Konami's Famicom follow-up Super C when that run-and-gun reached the NES in 1990. The cart rearranges the arcade sequel instead of copying its stages one for one.
life-force: Konami's Life Force is the Western name for Salamander, a 1986 shooter spun off from Gradius and set inside a living planet. The NES version mixes that organic look with a Gradius-style power bar.
after-burner: Yu Suzuki's After Burner is Sega's 1987 arcade jet game, and the deluxe cabinet tilted as the fighter rolled. Home ports exist, but the public identity is that coin-op, not an NES original.
monster-in-my-pocket: Konami's Monster in My Pocket brings the toy line of pocket-sized creatures to the NES in 1992. It is a side-scrolling license, unrelated to the later Pokemon games despite the similar phrase.
rampage: Bally Midway's Rampage, from 1986, lets the movie monsters George, Lizzie, and Ralph smash buildings and eat bystanders. The NES cart is a port of that arcade destruction.
nuts-milk: Hudson Soft's Nuts & Milk is an early Famicom maze chase from 1984, also sold on Japanese computers. One character flees with food while the other gives chase on single screens.
chase-hq: Taito's Chase H.Q. is a 1988 arcade drive about ramming a suspect's car before the timer expires. A radio dispatcher calls the briefing; home ports include an NES edition.
spy-hunter-1983: Bally Midway's Spy Hunter (1983) arms a car with oil, smoke, and missiles, set to a Peter Gunn-style theme. The NES port keeps the overhead highway combat of the arcade cabinet.
wrecking-crew-1985: Nintendo's Wrecking Crew (1985) sends Mario and Luigi to knock out walls on trap-filled demolition screens. It is a Famicom puzzle-action game, not the later Wrecking Crew '98.
samurai-pizza-cats: Samurai Pizza Cats takes its title from the English dub of the anime Kyatto Ninden Teyandee, about samurai cats. The Famicom game uses that Japanese series; it is a cartoon license, not an original mascot.
paperboy-2: Paperboy 2 moves the delivery route onto home consoles in 1991 and lets you ride as a papergirl as well as a paperboy. It is a home sequel, not a famous new arcade cabinet.
silent-service: Sid Meier designed Silent Service for MicroProse as a World War II submarine simulation on home computers in the mid-1980s. The NES cartridge is a later port, not the original release.
bucky-ohare: Konami's Bucky O'Hare adapts the comic-and-cartoon hare for a 1992 NES action game that fans still rate highly. Bucky and his crew cross side-view stages on one of Konami's stronger licensed carts.
spy-vs-spy-2: First Star Software's Spy vs. Spy, based on Antonio Prohias's Mad magazine strip, splits the screen so two spies can trap one room. The 1984 computer game later reached the NES; it is not the Island Caper sequel.
gauntlet-1985: Ed Logg's Gauntlet (1985) for Atari Games is the four-player dungeon cabinet whose narrator warns that a hero is about to die. Wizard, Valkyrie, Warrior, and Elf are the original classes.
blades-of-steel-1988: Konami's Blades of Steel (1988) is an arcade hockey game whose dropped gloves turn into a separate punching match. The NES port keeps those fast periods and penalty brawls.
shatterhand: Natsume's Shatterhand reached American NES players through Jaleco in 1991 as a cyborg brawler. In Japan the same game licenses the tokusatsu series Tokkyuu Shirei Solbrain.
tetris-tengen: Tengen, Atari Games' NES label, shipped an unlicensed Tetris (Tengen) with a competitive mode and was forced to pull it from stores. Nintendo won the 1989 rights case, and its own licensed cart stayed.
rygar-1987: Tecmo's Rygar (1987) arms a warrior with a shield on a chain, the diskarmor. The NES game is a large side-view adventure, far bigger than the short looping arcade original.
terminator-2-judgment-day: Terminator 2: Judgment Day names several different games tied to the 1991 film, not one design. Midway's arcade cabinet is a light-gun shooter, while the NES and Game Boy carts are separate side-view licenses.
mitsume-ga-tooru: Mitsume ga Tooru adapts Osamu Tezuka's manga The Three-Eyed One to the Famicom in 1992. Natsume's Japanese action game did not receive a contemporary English NES release.
tiny-toon-adventures-2-trouble-in-wackyl: Konami's Tiny Toon Adventures 2: Trouble in Wackyland sends Buster into the cartoon's warped park on the NES in 1992. It continues Konami's first NES Tiny Toons cart, not the Super Nintendo game.
kings-quest-v: Roberta Williams's King's Quest V moved Sierra's series to point-and-click play and VGA graphics in 1990. The NES port is a notorious, stripped-down version of that computer adventure.
adventures-of-lolo-1989: HAL Laboratory's Adventures of Lolo (1989) is an Eggerland puzzle about pushing blocks, sealing monsters, and reaching the jewel chests. Lolo and Lala lead this NES chapter of a longer series.
yoshi: Nintendo's 1991 puzzle Yoshi, sold in Japan under an egg title, appeared on the NES and Game Boy. Mario stacks falling enemies until matched pairs vanish and a dinosaur hatches underneath.
space-harrier-1986: Yu Suzuki's Space Harrier (1986) is Sega's super-scaler arcade shooter, a checkered plain rushing toward a flying hero. An NES port exists, but it cannot match the cabinet that defined the game.
elevator-action-1983: Taito's Elevator Action (1983) is an arcade spy game of elevators, doorways, and stolen documents. The NES cartridge is a home port of that building raid.
crystalis: SNK's Crystalis is a 1990 NES action RPG set after a disaster, with swords tied to the elements. It is an original SNK quest, not a port of a computer RPG.
adventure-island-3: Hudson Soft's Takahashi Meijin no Bugutte Honey, from 1987, mixes side-scrolling with Breakout-style rooms and stars the company's spokesman. It is a Japan-only Famicom game, not an Adventure Island sequel.
toy-story: Traveller's Tales' Toy Story is the 1995 platformer based on the Pixar film, built for Super Nintendo and Genesis. A Game Boy edition exists, but it is not the same production as those 16-bit stages.
indiana-jones-and-the-last-crusade-1991: US Gold's Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade: The Action Game is the 1989 film's platformer, separate from Lucasfilm's point-and-click adventure. Tiered screens stand in for set pieces such as the circus train.
urban-champion-1984: Nintendo's Urban Champion (1984) is a simple Famicom fistfight on a sidewalk, often cited among the company's slight early games. Flower pots drop from windows while two fighters shove each other toward the street.
fantastic-dizzy: The Oliver twins' egg hero stars in Codemasters' Fantastic Dizzy, a 1991 puzzle adventure in the Dizzy line. Camerica later sold an unlicensed NES version; the game did not start as a Nintendo product.
rockin-kats: Atlus's Rockin' Kats sends a cartoon cat with a punching spring-gun through NES stages in 1991. It is an original Atlus platformer, not a licensed Saturday-morning cartoon.
adventure-island: Hudson's Adventure Island III (1992) continues Master Higgins's island crossing on the NES, dinosaur mounts included. It is the third Western entry, still descended from the Wonder Boy-derived original.
baseball-1983: Nintendo's Baseball (1983) is an early Famicom sports game, a simple diamond viewed from behind the plate. The later Game Boy Baseball is another cartridge in Nintendo's sports line, not this same code.
ultima-4-quest-of-the-avatar: Richard Garriott's Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar, published by Origin in 1985, asks the player to live out eight virtues. The NES port is a later adaptation of that computer RPG.
pac-man: Toru Iwatani's Pac-Man, from Namco in 1980, clears mazes of dots while four ghosts give chase. The Famicom port came years later; the public identity is the arcade craze, not a Nintendo debut.
battle-city: Namco's Battle City is a 1985 Famicom tank game descended from Tank Battalion, built so two players can share one screen. It was a Japanese hit and reached many Western players only in later reissues.
contra-1987: Konami's Contra (1987) is the run-and-gun Europe called Gryzor, and the NES version became a co-op benchmark. That home cart is tied to the Konami code's extra lives and rearranges the arcade stages.
alwas-awakening: Alwa's Awakening is a 2017 indie adventure sold for PC and as a physical NES cartridge. It is new software written for the old console, not a rerelease of a licensed 1980s game.
chips-challenge: Chuck Sommerville's Chip's Challenge debuted on the Atari Lynx in 1989, a top-down puzzle of keys, computer chips, and monsters. Microsoft later bundled it in a Windows Entertainment Pack.
metal-gear: Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear began on the MSX2 in 1987 as a sneaking mission rather than a straight shooter. The NES version changes maps and bosses, and Kojima has distanced himself from that port.
duck-hunt-1984: Nintendo's Duck Hunt (1984) pairs the NES Zapper with a dog that laughs when you miss. It shipped in the Action Set beside Super Mario Bros., which made the clay pigeons a pack-in memory.
chip-n-dale-rescue-rangers: Capcom's Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers lets the two chipmunks pick up and throw objects, enemies included, in a 1990 NES platformer. It is based on the Disney Afternoon series.
final-fantasy-1987: Hironobu Sakaguchi's Final Fantasy (1987) is Square's Famicom RPG of the four Light Warriors, the game that launched the series. North America received Nintendo's localization two years later.
chip-n-dale-rescue-rangers-2: Capcom's Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers 2 returns the chipmunks to the NES in 1993 and adds a shop between stages. Throwing enemies, the hook of the first Disney Afternoon cart, remains.
dyna-blaster: Hudson Soft's Bomberman (1983) began as a computer maze game and became a Famicom staple about a robot placing bombs. Europe often sold later entries under the Dynablaster name.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-iii-the-man: Konami's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III: The Manhattan Project is a 1991 NES brawler, not a port of the arcade game. Its story takes the turtles through Manhattan instead of repeating the coin-op.
ducktales: Capcom's Disney's DuckTales sends Scrooge pogo-hopping on his cane through NES treasure hunts in 1989. It remains one of the best-known Disney games on that console.
altered-beast-1988: Sega's Altered Beast (1988) opens with a call to rise from the grave and turns a centurion into beasts as he grabs spirit balls. It was an arcade game and a Genesis pack-in; the NES cart is a later port.
the-jungle-book: Virgin Interactive's Disney's The Jungle Book is a platformer of the animated film, with Mowgli crossing levels built around the songs. Genesis and Super Nintendo versions are the main 16-bit releases.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-1989: Konami's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (1989) is the demanding NES adventure with the dam, swimming sections, and a top-down overworld. It is not the arcade beat 'em up, which a later cart ported.
maniac-mansion: Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick's Maniac Mansion, from Lucasfilm Games in 1987, introduced the SCUMM scripting system for graphic adventures. Jaleco's NES port censors some of the mansion's jokes.
arkanoid-1986: Taito's Arkanoid (1986) rebuilds Breakout around the Vaus craft, capsule power-ups, and a short escape story. The NES edition can use a dedicated paddle controller in place of the pad.
star-trek-25th-anniversary: Interplay's Star Trek: 25th Anniversary marks the show's silver jubilee around 1991. The computer release is a point-and-click voyage, with the original cast on the CD edition, while the NES cart is a more action-led tie-in.
the-little-mermaid: Capcom's The Little Mermaid is an NES platformer based on Disney's film, with Ariel in swimming and walking stages. It is not the same game as the Genesis Little Mermaid from another developer.
battle-chess: Interplay's Battle Chess, from 1988, follows chess rules but animates every capture as a fight between the pieces. The NES version is a home port of that computer novelty.
popeye: Nintendo's Popeye is a 1982 arcade license: the sailor gathers Olive Oyl's tokens before Bluto catches him, and spinach is a short power-up. An NES port of that coin-op is real.
dig-dug-1982: In Namco's Dig Dug (1982), Taizo pumps Pookas and Fygars with air until they burst, or drops rocks on them. Later games treat the digger as Mr. Driller's father.
captain-america-and-the-avengers: Data East's Captain America and The Avengers is a 1991 arcade brawler featuring the Marvel team. NES and Super Nintendo releases are separate home versions, not one identical port.
hillsfar-1993: SSI's Hillsfar (1993) is a Forgotten Realms spinoff of arena fights, lockpicking, and errands in the city. It started on computers in the late 1980s; the NES edition is a later cartridge.
dragon-quest-1986: Enix's Dragon Quest (1986), by Yuji Horii with Toriyama, Sugiyama, and Chunsoft, set the template for Japanese console RPGs. North America received it in 1989 as Dragon Warrior.
double-dragon-3-the-rosetta-stone: Technos' NES game Double Dragon III: The Sacred Stones (1991) changes the arcade subtitle, which was The Rosetta Stone. Billy and Jimmy still fight, but the home version is its own quest.
smash-tv: Eugene Jarvis's Smash TV, from Williams in 1990, is a twin-stick arcade shooter staged as a lethal game show. NES and Super Nintendo ports followed the cabinet's room-by-room prize grab.
game-1942: Capcom's 1942 is a 1984 arcade shooter set over the Pacific, the first of the studio's wartime 19XX series. The NES port keeps the looping Super Ace and the same vertical scroll.
ms-pac-man: General Computer Corporation built Ms. Pac-Man for Midway, a sequel with wandering mazes and a bow on the hero. It followed Pac-Man in the early 1980s and was not a Namco design; Nintendo ports came much later.
robocop-versus-the-terminator: RoboCop Versus The Terminator adapts the Dark Horse comic crossover rather than a film team-up. Virgin's Genesis game is the best-known version; Super Nintendo and NES editions are separate carts.
jackal-1986: Konami's Jackal (1986), also called Top Gunner, drives a jeep behind enemy lines to rescue prisoners. The NES version is a port of that overhead arcade shooter.
ninja-gaiden-iii-the-ancient-ship-of-doo: Tecmo's Ninja Gaiden III: The Ancient Ship of Doom (1991) closes the NES trilogy with story scenes between stages. Ryu Hayabusa returns, and the US cartridge is stricter about continues than the Japanese one.
wolverine: LJN's Wolverine is a 1991 NES action game starring the Marvel mutant. It belongs to that publisher's comic licenses, not to the later fighting-game appearances.
final-fantasy-iii-1990: Square's Final Fantasy III (1990) is the Famicom game that introduced a full job system and had no English release in its own era. The cartridge North America once called Final Fantasy III is actually VI.
adventure-island-ii-1991: Hudson's Adventure Island II (1991) gives Master Higgins dinosaur companions on the NES. It is the first sequel, still a side-view island trek rather than a new kind of game.
karateka-1986: Jordan Mechner's Karateka (1985) is the Apple II martial-arts game he made before Prince of Persia, published by Broderbund. The computer original is from 1984; an NES port came later.
rushn-attack: The NES Rush'n Attack is Konami's home version of the arcade Green Beret, a base assault fought largely with a knife. It is the American name; the coin-op predates the cartridge.
robocop-3: Robocop 3 licenses the third film on NES and Super Nintendo cartridges that do not play alike. Both are early-1990s tie-ins, and neither is Data East's earlier arcade RoboCop.
kunio-kun-no-nekketsu-soccer-league: Technos' Kunio-kun no Nekketsu Soccer League is a 1993 Famicom soccer game in the Kunio-kun series. It stayed in Japan, whereas Nintendo World Cup had exported an earlier Nekketsu soccer title.
ninja-gaiden-ii-the-dark-sword-of-chaos: Tecmo's Ninja Gaiden II: The Dark Sword of Chaos (1990) continues Ryu's NES story with cinema-style scenes between stages. New blades and wind-tossed platforms join that cutscene format.
donkey-kong-3: Nintendo's Donkey Kong 3 replaces Jumpman with Stanley, an exterminator spraying bugs at Donkey Kong in a greenhouse. The arcade original is from 1983 and is the odd third coin-op, not another climbing rescue.
gradius: Konami's Gradius, also sold as Nemesis, is the 1985 arcade shooter that introduced the Vic Viper's selectable power bar. The NES port is real and keeps that left-to-right upgrade path.
lunar-pool: Compile's Lunar Pool, called Lunar Ball in Japan, is a 1985 billiards game of oddly shaped tables and adjustable friction. It began on Japanese computers before the Famicom and NES releases.
micro-machines-old: Codemasters' Micro Machines (Old) is the 1991 tabletop racer based on the Galoob toys, sold on the NES as an unlicensed Camerica cart. Courses run across desks, pool tables, and breakfast leftovers.
the-flintstones-the-rescue-of-dino-hoppy: Taito's The Flintstones: The Rescue of Dino & Hoppy is an NES platformer based on the Hanna-Barbera cartoon, released in the US in 1991. Fred sets out to recover the kidnapped dinosaur and hopparoo.
tetris-1989: Nintendo's licensed NES cartridge Tetris (1989) is the one that remained after the Tengen lawsuit. It is distinct both from Pajitnov's original and from the unlicensed cart pulled off shelves.
tennis: Nintendo's Tennis is a Famicom singles-and-doubles game from 1984, programmed with help from HAL Laboratory. The NES cart came from that design, and a separate handheld edition followed later.
hogans-alley-1984: Nintendo's Hogan's Alley (1984) is a Zapper trainer: shoot the gangsters and spare the innocents. It shared the Famicom light-gun lineup with Duck Hunt and Wild Gunman.
simcity: Will Wright's SimCity, from Maxis in 1989, is the city builder about zoning, power, and disasters that started on computers. Nintendo later published an NES port and a richer Super Nintendo edition.
the-addams-family: Ocean's The Addams Family is a platformer based on the film, and the Super Nintendo version is remembered as a large, difficult mansion. The NES cartridge is a separate, smaller license.
joe-mac: Data East's Joe & Mac, also known as Caveman Ninja, is a 1991 arcade club-and-dinosaur brawler. The Super Nintendo version became the best-known home edition.
snake-rattle-n-roll: Rare's Snake Rattle 'n' Roll is an isometric NES game about two snakes eating Nibbley Pibbles until they weigh enough to ring a bell. Rare also produced a Game Boy version.
resident-evil-2: Capcom's Resident Evil 2 (1998) follows Leon Kennedy and Claire Redfield through Raccoon City on PlayStation. The Nintendo 64 port is famous for fitting that two-disc game onto one cartridge.
quake: id Software's Quake, from 1996, is the fully 3D follow-up to DOOM, with a soundtrack credited to Trent Reznor. A Nintendo 64 port came after the PC original.
worms-armageddon: Team17's Worms Armageddon, from 1999, is widely treated as the high point of the 2D artillery series, with a deep editor and a huge weapon list. Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color editions port that PC design.
quake-2: id Software's Quake II, from 1997, turns the series into a war against the Strogg on an alien world. The Nintendo 64 release is a later port, with its own compromises in lighting and geometry.
daikatana: Ion Storm's John Romero's Daikatana reached PC in 2000 after years of hype and became a notorious critical failure. Kemco's Nintendo 64 port followed and was received even more harshly.
turok: Acclaim and Iguana's Turok: Dinosaur Hunter brings the comic hero to the Nintendo 64 in 1997, foggy jungles and all. It was one of that console's early first-person showpieces.
starcraft: Blizzard's StarCraft, released in 1998, is the real-time war of Terran, Zerg, and Protoss. Nintendo published a Nintendo 64 port that adds a console-only episode.
turok-2-seeds-of-evil: Acclaim's Turok 2: Seeds of Evil continues the Nintendo 64 dinosaur hunting in 1998, darker levels and the cerebral bore included. Iguana developed it as a sequel, not a fresh license.
hexen-for-windows-95: Raven Software's HeXen: Beyond Heretic is the 1995 fantasy shooter sequel to Heretic, with three character classes and hub levels. It began on PC; the Nintendo 64 version is a later port.
doom-64: Midway's Doom 64 is an original 1997 Nintendo 64 campaign, not a straight port of the PC episodes. New maps and a more ambient score set it apart from the Super Nintendo DOOM cartridge.
spider-man-2000: Neversoft's Spider-Man (2000), published by Activision, is the third-person game narrated by Stan Lee. It launched on PlayStation and also reached the Nintendo 64; it is not the later movie game.
tony-hawks-pro-skater-2: Neversoft's Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 2 adds manuals and custom parks to the skateboarding hit in 2000. The Nintendo 64 version follows the PlayStation design; the Game Boy Color edition is a separate 2D game.
star-wars-rogue-squadron-3d: Factor 5's STAR WARS: Rogue Squadron 3D is a 1998 Nintendo 64 flight game of Rebel missions, published with LucasArts. Speeder runs and starfighter sorties share one campaign.
shadow-man: Acclaim's Shadow Man adapts the Valiant comic for a 1999 action-adventure, with the Nintendo 64 among its platforms. Mike LeRoi crosses between Liveside and Deadside.
rayman-2-the-great-escape: Michel Ancel and Ubisoft's Rayman 2: The Great Escape moves Rayman into 3D in 1999, and the Nintendo 64 edition is among the best regarded. It is a different game from the original side-view Rayman.
star-wars-shadows-of-the-empire: LucasArts' Star Wars: Shadows of the Empire, from 1996, fills the gap between The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi as a multimedia project. Dash Rendar's Nintendo 64 game includes the Battle of Hoth.
super-smash-bros-1999: HAL Laboratory and Masahiro Sakurai's Super Smash Bros. (1999) knocks Nintendo characters off platforms instead of draining a life bar. It is the first game in the series and a Nintendo 64 original.
mortal-kombat-4: Midway's Mortal Kombat 4 takes the tournament into polygons in 1997, the first main entry to leave sprites behind. The Nintendo 64 version is a home port of that arcade shift.
goldeneye-007-1997: Rare's GoldenEye 007 (1997) turns the James Bond film into a Nintendo 64 shooter whose split-screen matches reshaped console multiplayer. Rare developed it and Nintendo published it.
disneys-tarzan: Disney's Tarzan is a 1999 platformer based on Disney's animated film, released on the Nintendo 64 and PlayStation. Vine swings and the movie's set pieces lead, rather than a straight adaptation of the Burroughs novels.
carmageddon: Stainless Games' Carmageddon, published by SCI in 1997, is a car-combat racer notorious for running over pedestrians. A Nintendo 64 port exists and was censored in some regions; the PC game is the original.
tony-hawks-pro-skater-3: Neversoft's Tony Hawk's Pro Skater 3 adds the revert and a deeper park editor in 2001. PlayStation 2 led; the Nintendo 64 edition is a later, reduced version of the same skateboarding design.
donkey-kong-64: Rare's Donkey Kong 64 brings DK, Diddy, Tiny, Lanky, and Chunky to the Nintendo 64 in 1999, and it requires the Expansion Pak. It is a 3D collect-a-thon follow-up to the Country series, not a port of the arcade game.
star-wars-episode-i-racer: LucasArts' STAR WARS: Episode I Racer is the 1999 podracing game spun out of The Phantom Menace. Nintendo 64 and PC versions are the main releases; the Game Boy Color cart is a much simpler spinoff.
tony-hawks-pro-skater: Neversoft's Tony Hawk's Pro Skater, published by Activision in 1999, turns real skaters and timed tricks into a console sport. It debuted on PlayStation; the Nintendo 64 version followed.
indiana-jones-and-the-infernal-machine: LucasArts' Indiana Jones and the Infernal Machine is a 3D adventure that debuted on PC, with a Nintendo 64 port in 2000. It is not one of the earlier Last Crusade games.
earthworm-jim-3d: Earthworm Jim 3D moves the worm into a Nintendo 64 platformer in 1999, made by a different team than Shiny's side-scrollers. Reviews were much colder than they had been for the 16-bit games.
super-mario-all-stars-1993: Nintendo's Super Mario All-Stars (1993) remakes Super Mario Bros., the Japanese Lost Levels, Super Mario Bros. 2, and Super Mario Bros. 3 for the Super Nintendo. It is a compilation, not a new adventure.
the-lost-vikings: Silicon & Synapse's The Lost Vikings, published by Interplay in 1993, switches among Erik, Baleog, and Olaf, each with a different tool. That studio later became Blizzard.
street-fighter-2: Capcom's Street Fighter II: The World Warrior (1991) revived arcade one-on-one fighting and defined the six-button layout. The Super Nintendo port became a landmark home version of that roster.
secret-of-mana-1993: Square's Secret of Mana (1993), Seiken Densetsu 2 in Japan, is a Super Famicom action RPG with a ring menu and room for three players. Cooperative play is the feature people still cite.
populous: Peter Molyneux and Bullfrog's Populous, from 1989, is the god game of raising land so a population can expand and fight. Console ports, including Super Nintendo, followed the computer original.
flashback-1992: Delphine's Flashback: The Quest for Identity, led by Paul Cuisset, is a 1992 cinematic platformer about an amnesiac named Conrad. It followed Another World and was strongest on computers and the Genesis.
teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-turtles-in-: Konami's Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles IV: Turtles in Time is the 1992 beat 'em up, a Super Nintendo reworking of the arcade game with extra stages. It is a high point of the studio's turtle brawlers.
drakkhen: Infogrames' Drakkhen is a late-1980s computer RPG that became an early North American Super Nintendo release. Its overworld uses a three-dimensional view unusual for RPGs of that moment.
desert-strike: Electronic Arts' Desert Strike is a 1992 helicopter campaign, first on the Genesis, inspired by contemporary desert warfare. The Super Nintendo version ports that isometric mission map.
cannon-fodder: Sensible Software's Cannon Fodder, from 1993, jokes that war has never been so much fun, then sends tiny soldiers onto a battlefield where they die for good. Jon Hare's team made it first for the Amiga.
fatal-fury-special: SNK's Fatal Fury Special is the 1993 upgrade of Fatal Fury 2, adding fighters and combo routes on Neo Geo. The Super Nintendo version is a home port of that revision.
samurai-shodown: SNK's Samurai Shodown is a 1993 weapon-based Neo Geo fighter, with Haohmaru among the swordsmen and a rage gauge that changes the duel. Super Nintendo and Game Boy ports followed the arcade game.
sunset-riders: Konami's Sunset Riders is a 1991 Wild West run-and-gun, four players in arcades and two on the Super Nintendo. Bounty targets are posted between towns; the home version is a port, not a new license.
pushover: Ocean's Pushover is a domino-toppling puzzle starring the ant G.I. Ant. Computer editions tied the puzzles to Britain's Quavers snacks; the Super Nintendo version swaps that branding for money bags.
sid-meiers-civilization: Sid Meier's Civilization, from MicroProse in 1991, starts a people in the ancient world and aims them toward space, one technology at a time. The Super Nintendo edition is a later port of that computer strategy game.
castlevania-rondo-of-blood-2: Konami's Castlevania: Rondo of Blood is a 1993 PC Engine Super CD game starring Richter Belmont and Maria Renard. It is not the Super Nintendo cartridge; that machine received the different Dracula X instead.
boogerman-a-pick-and-flick-adventure-199: Interplay's Boogerman: A Pick and Flick Adventure is a gross-out platformer whose hero attacks with burps and nose flicks. It shipped on Super Nintendo and Genesis in the mid-1990s.
wwf-wrestlemania-the-arcade-game: Midway's WWF WrestleMania: The Arcade Game uses digitized wrestlers and combo-heavy fights in a 1995 federation license. It is an arcade fighting take, not a simulation of a real pay-per-view card.
zombies-ate-my-neighbors-1993: LucasArts' Zombies Ate My Neighbors (1993) sends two kids through suburban horror-movie stages to rescue neighbors. Super Nintendo and Genesis were the original pair of releases.
kirby-super-star-1996: HAL and Masahiro Sakurai's Kirby Super Star (1996) packs several shorter games, including The Great Cave Offensive, onto one Super Nintendo cartridge. Japan calls the collection Kirby of the Stars Super Deluxe.
street-fighter-alpha-2: Capcom's Street Fighter Alpha 2, from 1996, adds custom combos to the prequel series set before Street Fighter II. The Super Nintendo port is a late, dense conversion of that arcade fighter.
contra-iii-the-alien-wars: Konami's Contra III: The Alien Wars is the 1992 Super Nintendo run-and-gun, known in Japan as Contra Spirits. Mode 7 set pieces and two-player play define it.
syndicate: Bullfrog's Syndicate, from 1993, is a cyberpunk tactics game of drugged corporate agents and a world map of hostile cities. The Super Nintendo cartridge ports that computer design.
mickey-mania: Mickey's Wild Adventure is the European PlayStation name for Traveller's Tales' Mickey Mania, a 1994 platformer through classic Mickey cartoons. The Super Nintendo and Genesis versions came first, under the Mania title.
jungle-strike: Electronic Arts' Jungle Strike is the 1993 follow-up to Desert Strike, still an isometric campaign, now with extra vehicles besides the helicopter. Super Nintendo and Game Boy versions came after the Genesis lead.
batman-forever: Acclaim's Batman Forever is a 1995 action game based on the Joel Schumacher film. Super Nintendo and Game Boy carts share that movie license, not Sunsoft's earlier Batman games.
mega-man-x2: Capcom's Mega Man X2, from 1994, continues the Super Nintendo X series with the X-Hunters holding pieces of Zero. Whether those parts are recovered changes if Zero can return to help.
populous-2-trials-of-the-olympian-gods: Bullfrog's Populous 2: Trials of the Olympian Gods moves the god game into Greek myth in 1991. Divine effects and a pantheon of rivals set it apart from the first Populous.
super-ghoulsn-ghosts: Capcom's Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts (1991) is the Super Nintendo sequel, with Arthur dashing through a harder monster gauntlet. Japan knows it as Chou Makaimura; it follows the arcade Ghouls 'n Ghosts.
street-fighter-ii-turbo-hyper-fighting: Capcom's Street Fighter II Turbo: Hyper Fighting speeds the cast up and adds new special moves, an arcade revision from 1992. The Super Nintendo port let players use that faster ruleset at home.
shin-megami-tensei-ii: Atlus's Shin Megami Tensei II continues the Super Famicom apocalypse in 1994, with an underground Tokyo and alignment choices. It is a mainline sequel, not the school spinoff If.
mario-paint: Nintendo's Mario Paint, from 1992, is a Super Nintendo drawing toy bundled with a mouse. Stamps, animation, and a music composer sit beside a fly-swatting minigame.
ultima-vi-the-false-prophet: Origin's Ultima VI: The False Prophet, from 1990, continues Richard Garriott's Avatar in a gargoyle conflict on PC. The Super Nintendo release is a later, heavily altered home version.
star-ocean: tri-Ace and Enix's Star Ocean is the 1996 Super Famicom debut of the series, mixing real-time fights with private actions in town. It stayed Japan-only until much later remakes.
disneys-aladdin: Capcom's Disney’s Aladdin (1993) is the Super Nintendo platformer, a different production from Virgin's Genesis Aladdin. It uses Capcom's own stages rather than Virgin's animation-heavy design.
wild-guns-1994: Natsume's Wild Guns (1994) is a Super Nintendo gallery shooter set in a steampunk Wild West, and two players can share the screen. It is an original Natsume design, not a light-gun port of an older coin-op.
starfox-2: Argonaut and Nintendo finished Starfox 2 for the Super Nintendo in the mid-1990s, then shelved it. The official release finally came in 2017 on the Super NES Classic Edition.
super-bomberman-2: Hudson's Super Bomberman 2 is a 1994 Super Nintendo maze game whose story mode is about capturing the bomber. Multitap matches remain the reason people kept the cart.
international-superstar-soccer: Konami's International Superstar Soccer on the Super Nintendo, from 1994, is the celebrated first game in that soccer line. Later consoles received their own follow-ups rather than one unchanged port.
venomspider-man-separation-anxiety: Acclaim's Venom/Spider-Man: Separation Anxiety is the beat 'em up sequel to Maximum Carnage, again starring the symbiote pair. Software Creations developed the mid-1990s Super Nintendo and Genesis versions.
dungeon-master: FTL Games' Dungeon Master, from 1987, is the real-time first-person crawl that became a hit on the Atari ST. A Super Nintendo port arrived years later; the ST game is the one that shook the genre.
super-bomberman-3: Hudson's Super Bomberman 3 supports five players on the Super Nintendo in 1995 and themes its stages around world cities. It continues the multitap party design of the earlier Super Bomberman carts.
shin-megami-tensei-if: Atlus's Shin Megami Tensei If... is the 1994 Super Famicom spinoff set in a demon-invaded high school. That school premise later fed the Persona series.
front-mission: Square's Front Mission: The First (1995) is the Super Famicom strategy RPG of customizable wanzer mechs. Later remakes reused the subtitle The First for this same story.
pilotwings-1990: Nintendo's Pilotwings (1990) is a Super Famicom launch title of biplanes, hang gliders, and skydiving lessons. It shows off Mode 7 flight rather than combat sorties.
sailor-moon: Angel's Bishoujo Senshi Sailor Moon (1993) is a Super Famicom side-scrolling brawler based on the anime, with the Sailor Soldiers as the playable cast. A later R follow-up added a one-on-one mode this first cart lacks.
fatal-fury-king-of-fighters: SNK's Fatal Fury: King of Fighters is the 1991 Neo Geo fighter that introduced Terry Bogard and the King of Fighters tournament. The Super Nintendo version ports that first Fatal Fury, not a later KOF entry.
pirates-of-dark-water: Pirates of Dark Water is a 1994 Super Nintendo action game based on the Hanna-Barbera series. It is a cartoon license about Ren's quest, not an original pirate design.
gods: The Bitmap Brothers' Gods is a 1991 platformer known for ornate graphics and a shop between levels. It began on the Amiga and later received a Super Nintendo port.
fifa-international-soccer: EA Sports' first association-football game, FIFA International Soccer, reached consoles in 1993 with an isometric pitch that stood out from top-down soccer. Extended Play Productions developed that debut.
ogre-battle-the-march-of-the-black-queen: Quest and Yasumi Matsuno's Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen is a 1993 Super Famicom strategy RPG of real-time squads and moral alignment. It is the first Ogre Battle, not Tactics Ogre.
tiny-toon-adventures-buster-busts-loose: Konami's Tiny Toon Adventures: Buster Busts Loose! is the 1992 Super Nintendo platformer, sports stages and a football finale included. It is separate from Konami's NES Tiny Toons carts.
bubsy: Accolade's Bubsy, fully titled Claws Encounters of the Furred Kind, is a 1993 bobcat platformer on Super Nintendo and Genesis. Michael Berlyn's speedy mascot was heavily promoted and later widely mocked.
super-star-wars-the-empire-strikes-back: LucasArts' Super Star Wars: The Empire Strikes Back continues the Super Nintendo film trilogy in 1993, Hoth included. Sculptured Software again built the action between movie set pieces.
the-lost-vikings-2: Blizzard's The Lost Vikings 2, also called Norse by Norsewest, reunites the three Vikings on the Super Nintendo in 1997 and teaches them new skills. It is a much later sequel, not a companion to the first game's launch.
art-of-fighting-1992: SNK's Art of Fighting (1992) introduces Ryo Sakazaki and a spirit gauge that powers special moves on Neo Geo. The Super Nintendo port is a home version of that first entry.
spider-man-1995: Spider-Man (1995) is a side-scrolling Super Nintendo game based on Marvel's hero, one of several mid-decade carts that share the name. It is not Neversoft's later 3D Spider-Man.
stargate: Williams' Stargate, designed with Eugene Jarvis and released in 1981, is the arcade sequel to Defender and was later sold as Defender II. It is a space shooter, not a Super Nintendo platformer and not the 1994 film.
fatal-fury-2-1992: SNK's Fatal Fury 2 (1992) expands the Bogard brothers' tournament with a larger Neo Geo roster. Super Nintendo and Game Boy ports brought that sequel home.
aero-the-acro-bat: Sunsoft published Aero the Acro-Bat in 1993, a circus-bat platformer developed by Iguana Entertainment. Super Nintendo and Genesis versions star the bat working an amusement park.
nhl-98: EA Sports' NHL 98 is the hockey annual branded a year ahead of its release window, with a late Super Nintendo edition beside the 32-bit games. It belongs to EA's NHL line, not to Nintendo's Ice Hockey.
biker-mice-from-mars-1994: Biker Mice from Mars (SNES) licenses the animated mice for a 1994 Super Nintendo motorcycle combat game. The hardware tag in the name marks this 16-bit cart, not a later remake.
blast-corps: Rare's Blast Corps, from 1997, clears a path for a runaway nuclear carrier by smashing buildings with trucks and robots. It is a Nintendo 64 original from the studio behind GoldenEye, not a licensed disaster film.
glover: Hasbro Interactive's Glover is a 1998 Nintendo 64 platformer about a magic glove guiding a ball that can change form. Play revolves around bowling, bouncing, and carrying that ball.
40-winks: Eurocom's 40 Winks is a 1999 PlayStation platformer about rescuing dream spirits called Winks. A Nintendo 64 version was cancelled at the time and only surfaced many years later.
castlevania-1998: Konami's Castlevania (1999), often called Castlevania 64, is the Nintendo 64's 3D entry starring Reinhardt Schneider and Carrie Fernandez. It is a new quest, not a port of Symphony of the Night.
pokemon-puzzle-league-2000: Nintendo's Pokémon Puzzle League (2000) applies Panel de Pon matching to Pokemon characters on the Nintendo 64. The US version uses voices from the 4Kids anime dub.
nuclear-strike: Electronic Arts' Nuclear Strike is the 1997 entry in the Strike helicopter series, moving the campaign into fuller 3D. The Nintendo 64 version followed the PlayStation and PC releases.
nhl-99: EA Sports' NHL 99 carries the annual hockey series onto the Nintendo 64 under 1998 season branding. It is a 3D EA hockey game, not a sequel to Konami's Blades of Steel.
cruisn-usa-1996: Midway's Cruis'n USA (1996) is the cross-country racer Nintendo also shipped on the Nintendo 64 near that console's launch. The arcade cabinet came before the home cart.
world-cup-98-2: EA Sports' World Cup 98 is the officially licensed game of the FIFA World Cup held in France in 1998. Nintendo 64 and Game Boy editions sit beside the PlayStation and PC releases.
micro-machines-v3: Codemasters' Micro Machines V3 moves the toy-car races into 3D in 1997, still across household surfaces. The Nintendo 64 version is one of several home ports of that third main entry.
batman-beyond-return-of-the-joker: Batman Beyond: Return of the Joker is a 2000 Nintendo 64 action game based on the animated film, not on Sunsoft's earlier NES Return of the Joker. It uses the futuristic Batman Beyond setting.
forsaken: Probe's Forsaken, published by Acclaim in 1998, is a six-degrees-of-freedom shooter in the vein of Descent. The Nintendo 64 version is a home port of that PC and PlayStation design.
mystical-ninja-starring-goemon-1997: Konami's Mystical Ninja Starring Goemon (1997) brings the long-running Goemon to the Nintendo 64, including a giant-robot musical stage fans still quote. The US release followed the Japanese Ganbare Goemon cart.
castlevania-legacy-of-darkness: Konami's Castlevania: Legacy of Darkness expands the Nintendo 64 Castlevania in 1999, adding Cornell the werewolf and revised levels. It works as both a prequel story and a reworking of the earlier 3D game.
sin-punishment: Treasure's Sin and Punishment - Successor of the Earth is a Nintendo 64 rail shooter published in Japan in 2000. Western players got an official English release later, including a 2007 Virtual Console edition.
tiggers-honey-hunt: Disney's Tigger's Honey Hunt is a 2000 platformer based on Disney's Winnie the Pooh characters, on Nintendo 64 and PlayStation. Tigger collects honey across levels spun from that franchise.
gauntlet-legends: Atari Games' Gauntlet Legends updates the four-hero dungeon crawl as a 3D arcade game in the late 1990s. The Nintendo 64 version ports that sequel, not the 1985 cabinet.
south-park-rally: Acclaim's South Park Rally is a 1999 kart racer using the Comedy Central cast. It is a separate Nintendo 64 license from the earlier South Park first-person game.
monster-truck-madness-2: Microsoft's Monster Truck Madness 2 is a 1998 PC racing sequel with licensed monster trucks and muddy tracks. It belongs to the Windows series that began with the earlier Monster Truck Madness.
ogre-battle-64-person-of-lordly-caliber: Quest's Ogre Battle 64: Person of Lordly Caliber continues the series on the Nintendo 64, with a 1999 Japanese release. Real-time squad battles remain, wrapped in a larger class story.
killer-instinct-gold: Rare's Killer Instinct Gold is the 1996 Nintendo 64 version of Killer Instinct 2, training mode included. It covers the sequel, not the earlier Super Nintendo Killer Instinct cart.
tonic-trouble: Ubisoft's Tonic Trouble is a 3D platformer about a clumsy alien who spills a magic drink on Earth, from the Rayman team. It drew much harsher reviews than Rayman 2.
bomberman-hero-1998: Hudson's Bomberman Hero (1998) turns the bomber into a Nintendo 64 platform-game hero instead of locking him to maze battles. It is a spinoff, not a numbered Super Bomberman port.
quest-64: Imagineer's Quest 64 is a 1998 Nintendo 64 RPG published by THQ in the US and as Holy Magic Century in Europe. It is one of the few RPGs on that console, and a divisive one, with a lone hero and no traditional party.
ready-2-rumble-boxing: Midway's Ready 2 Rumble Boxing is a 1999 cartoon boxing game built around exaggerated fighters such as Afro Thunder. Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color versions followed the arcade-style original.
snowboard-kids: Atlus's Snowboard Kids is a 1998 Nintendo 64 downhill racer that mixes courses with item attacks. It plays more like a cartoon kart race than a simulation of the sport.
hydro-thunder-1999: Midway's Hydro Thunder (1999) is an arcade powerboat racer full of jumps and boost starts. The Nintendo 64 version is a home port of that cabinet, not an original Nintendo water game.
army-men-air-attack: 3DO's Army Men: Air Attack (1999) puts plastic-green helicopters over backyard battlefields. It is a spinoff of the Army Men toy-soldier series, and the Nintendo 64 edition is one home port.
duke-nukem-zero-hour: Eurocom's Duke Nukem: Zero Hour is a 1999 Nintendo 64 third-person shooter with a time-travel plot, published by GT Interactive. It is not Duke Nukem 64, the port of Duke Nukem 3D.
ready-2-rumble-boxing-round-2: Midway's Ready 2 Rumble Boxing: Round 2 is the 2000 sequel, with a larger roster and the same exaggerated boxing. The Nintendo 64 version continues those cartoon bouts.
excitebike-64-2000: Left Field Productions' Excitebike 64 (2000), published by Nintendo, is a 3D dirt-bike follow-up in spirit to the NES Excitebike. A track editor and stunt racing keep it from being a simple remake.
turok-3-shadow-of-oblivion: Acclaim's Turok 3: Shadow of Oblivion closes the Nintendo 64 trilogy in 2000, with Danielle and Joseph as the hunters. It follows Seeds of Evil rather than restarting the comic license.
extreme-g: Probe's Extreme-G, published by Acclaim in 1997, is a futuristic Nintendo 64 motorcycle racer with weapons mounted on the bikes. Sequels on the same console followed it.
bomberman-64-the-second-attack: Hudson's Bomberman 64: The Second Attack is the 2000 Nintendo 64 sequel, known in Japan as a numbered follow-up to Bomberman 64. Adventure stages share space with the series' bombs.
goemons-great-adventure: Konami's Goemon's Great Adventure is the 1998 Nintendo 64 follow-up to Mystical Ninja, known in Japan as a Ganbare Goemon sequel. It shifts to a side-on view and keeps the series' jokes.
battlezone-1998: Activision's Battlezone (1998) reworks the Atari name into a PC game that mixes tank combat with base building. The Nintendo 64 release is a later, less famous port of that remake.
rugrats-in-paris-the-movie: Rugrats in Paris: The Movie is a 2000 licensed game based on the Nickelodeon film, with a Nintendo 64 version among the tie-ins. It uses the movie's Paris trip rather than an earlier Rugrats game-show setting.
animaniacs: Konami's Animaniacs turns the Warner Bros. cartoon into a 1994 platformer on Super Nintendo and Game Boy. Yakko, Wakko, and Dot share the license, and the two cartridges are not the same game.
breath-of-fire-ii: Capcom's Breath of Fire II (1994) is the Super Famicom sequel remembered for building a township between quests. It continues the dragon-transformation line started by the first game.
trials-of-mana-2: Square's Trials of Mana began as Seiken Densetsu 3 on the Super Famicom in 1995, and you choose three heroes from six. It had no official English release until the much later remake that uses this title.
goof-troop: Capcom's Goof Troop is a 1993 Super Nintendo cooperative game based on the Disney series, starring Goofy and Max. Two players solve rooms together; it is closer to a puzzle adventure than a cartoon brawler.
live-a-live: Square's Live A Live, directed by Takashi Tokita, is a 1994 Super Famicom RPG told as separate chapters across wildly different eras. An official English script waited until the HD-2D remake decades later.
castlevania-dracula-x: Konami's Castlevania: Dracula X is the 1995 Super Nintendo game, a different and more limited project than the PC Engine's Rondo of Blood. Richter still faces Dracula, but the stages are not the CD game's.
columns-1990: Sega's Columns (1990) matches jewels dropped in sets of three, a puzzle associated with the Genesis as a rival to falling blocks. It began as a computer and arcade design, not as a Super Nintendo original.
final-fight-2: Capcom's Final Fight 2 is a 1993 Super Nintendo sequel that never had an arcade cabinet. Haggar returns with new partners, Maki and Carlos, in Metro City.
ultima-vii-the-black-gate: Origin's Ultima VII: The Black Gate, from 1992, is Richard Garriott's sprawling mouse-driven chapter of Britannia on PC. A Super Nintendo game using the subtitle is a separate, much simpler adaptation.
super-bomberman: Hudson's Super Bomberman brought four-player maze battles to the Super Nintendo in 1993 through the multitap. That cart is what made Bomberman a 16-bit party fixture.
fifa-97: EA Sports' FIFA 97 is the soccer annual aimed at the 1996 season, still using an isometric pitch on the Super Nintendo. It continues the FIFA line rather than Konami's International Superstar Soccer.
toy-story-1995: Traveller's Tales' Toy Story (1995) is the Super Nintendo and Genesis platformer of the Pixar film, with Woody crossing rendered stages. The Game Boy cart is a separate, smaller tie-in.
captain-commando: Capcom's Captain Commando is a 1991 arcade brawler about a future hero and three odd partners, one of them a baby in a mech. The Super Nintendo version is a port of that coin-op.
final-fight-3: Capcom's Final Fight 3 is the 1995 Super Nintendo continuation, adding a super-move gauge and new allies in Metro City. Like Final Fight 2, it has no matching arcade cabinet.
top-gear-2: Top Gear 2 is the 1993 Super Nintendo racing sequel, adding weapons and a longer season to the first game's split-screen driving. Kemco published the series, known in Japan under the Top Racer name.
nba-jam-1994: Midway's NBA Jam (1994), developed with Mark Turmell, is the two-on-two basketball game famous for dunks and the announcer yelling that he's on fire. Arcades led, and it became a major home hit in 1993.
doom-troopers-mutant-chronicles: Doom Troopers: Mutant Chronicles is a 1995 run-and-gun based on the Mutant Chronicles science-fiction setting. The similar first word does not make it id Software's DOOM.
mighty-morphin-power-rangers: Mighty Morphin Power Rangers licenses the Saban television series. The 1994 Super Nintendo version is a one-on-one fighter, while the Game Boy release is another, smaller tie-in.
adventures-of-batman-robin: Konami's The Adventures of Batman and Robin is a 1994 Super Nintendo game based on the animated series, mixing platform stages with Batmobile runs. It is separate from Sunsoft's NES Batman carts.
battletoads-in-battlemaniacs: Rare's Battletoads in Battlemaniacs is the 1994 Super Nintendo Battletoads game, still known for severe difficulty spikes. It is neither the NES original nor the Double Dragon crossover.
final-fantasy-mystic-quest-1992: Square's Final Fantasy Mystic Quest (1992) is a simplified RPG aimed at North America, released in Japan as Final Fantasy USA: Mystic Quest. It is not numbered among the main Final Fantasy games.
maui-mallard-in-cold-shadow: Disney's Maui Mallard in Cold Shadow casts Donald Duck as a hard-boiled detective in a 1996 platformer. Super Nintendo and Genesis versions exist, and some US packaging leads with Donald's name.
demolition-man: Demolition Man is a 1994 Super Nintendo action game based on the Sylvester Stallone film. Corridor gunfights mix with brawling, and it is a movie license rather than a Midway arcade port.
super-street-fighter-ii-the-new-challeng: Capcom's Super Street Fighter II: The New Challengers adds Cammy, Dee Jay, T. Hawk, and Fei Long in 1993. The Super Nintendo version brought those four newcomers home.
wing-commander: Chris Roberts's Wing Commander, from Origin in 1990, mixes cockpit missions with a branching story between flights. The Super Nintendo port is a later, simplified adaptation of the PC game.
the-simpsons-barts-nightmare: Acclaim's The Simpsons: Bart's Nightmare sends a sleeping Bart through sketch-like Super Nintendo stages in 1992. It does not continue the plot of the NES Space Mutants cartridge.
international-superstar-soccer-deluxe: Konami's International Superstar Soccer Deluxe is the 1995 Super Nintendo update, with more teams and refined matches. It builds on the first ISS game rather than on EA's FIFA.
mechwarrior-3050: BattleTech: A Game of Armored Combat is the Super Nintendo name used for MechWarrior 3050, an isometric BattleMech game published by Activision. You pilot a Mad Cat in FASA's BattleTech setting.
asterix-obelix: Asterix & Obelix licenses the French comic about the Gaulish village that resists Rome. The 1995 Super Nintendo and Game Boy games are tie-ins to that bande dessinee, not an American cartoon.
secret-of-evermore: Square's Redmond studio developed Secret of Evermore in 1995, an action RPG that was not designed in Japan and was not released there. A boy travels with a dog that changes shape, in the manner of Secret of Mana.
x-men-mutant-apocalypse: Capcom's X-Men: Mutant Apocalypse is a 1995 Super Nintendo brawler starring the Marvel team. It is side-view action, not the later arcade fighter X-Men: Children of the Atom.
sim-city: Nintendo's Super Nintendo Sim City adds an advisor named Dr. Wright and lets Bowser strike as a disaster. It is a special edition of Will Wright's city builder, not the plainer NES port.
top-gear: Kemco's Top Gear is a 1992 Super Nintendo split-screen racer, known in Japan as Top Racer. A password saves your place in a country-by-country season.
actraiser-1990: Quintet's ActRaiser (1990), published by Enix, alternates side-view battles with a god's-eye mode where you grow a civilization. It is a Super Nintendo original from that Enix-associated studio.
lufia-ii-rise-of-the-sinistrals: Neverland's Lufia II: Rise of the Sinistrals, published by Taito, is the 1995 Super Famicom prequel known for intricate puzzle rooms. The US release kept those dungeon puzzles as a main draw.
prehistorik-2-1993: Titus's Prehistorik 2 is a European caveman platformer brought to the Super Nintendo and Game Boy. The 1993 sequel stars a club-wielding hero of that series, not Data East's Joe & Mac.
prince-of-persia-2-the-shadow-and-the-fl: Jordan Mechner's Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame is the 1993 DOS sequel, with new palace intrigue and the same careful swordplay. A Super Nintendo port exists, but the PC game is the original.
romancing-saga-2-2017: Square's Romancing SaGa 2, led by Akitoshi Kawazu, is a 1993 Super Famicom RPG about an empire passed down across generations. It did not receive a contemporary English release.
spider-man-and-venom-maximum-carnage: LJN's Spider-Man and Venom: Maximum Carnage adapts the comic crossover as a 1994 beat 'em up on Super Nintendo and Genesis. A red cartridge and the symbiote team-up are its public hooks.
mega-man-x3-1995: Capcom's Mega Man X3 (1995) continues the Super Nintendo X series under Dr. Doppler, and some versions let you play as Zero. It is the third X game, still a 16-bit run before later disc ports.
umihara-kawase: Umihara Kawase is a 1994 Super Famicom platformer whose stretchy fishing line is used to swing, grab, and climb. The first edition stayed in Japan and later picked up a cult following.
clock-tower: Human Entertainment's Clock Tower (1995), directed by Hifumi Kono, is a Super Famicom point-and-click horror game starring Jennifer and the Scissorman. It is a suspense adventure, not an action castle crawl.
cool-spot: Virgin's Cool Spot stars the 7 Up mascot in a 1993 platformer on Genesis and Super Nintendo. The red dot hops through bright levels that began as a soda mascot.
tactics-ogre-let-us-cling-together: Quest's Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together, directed by Yasumi Matsuno, is the 1995 Super Famicom tactical RPG. Battles sit on a grid, which sets it apart from the real-time Ogre Battle.
judge-dredd: Judge Dredd licenses the 2000 AD comic character for action games timed with the Stallone film in 1995. Super Nintendo and Game Boy carts share the name as movie-era tie-ins.
final-fight: Capcom's Final Fight is the 1989 arcade brawler in which Haggar, Cody, and Guy try to clean up Metro City. The first Super Nintendo port dropped two-player play and, at first, Guy.
killer-instinct-1994: Rare's Killer Instinct (1994) is the arcade fighter Nintendo promoted with combo breakers and a rock soundtrack. The Super Nintendo port is a reduced home version; Killer Instinct Gold later covered the sequel.
mega-man-7: Capcom's Mega Man 7 (1995) moves the classic blue hero to the Super Nintendo and introduces Bass as a rival. It continues the NES story rather than the separate Mega Man X timeline.
urban-strike: Electronic Arts' Urban Strike is the 1994 sequel that brings the Strike helicopter series into a city campaign. It followed Jungle Strike and still uses that series' mission map.
civilization: The Super Nintendo Civilization is a console port of Sid Meier's turn-based history game from MicroProse. You still chase technologies toward space, one more turn at a time, on a smaller home map.
frogger-1981: Konami's Frogger (1981) hops a frog through traffic and across a river, one of the simple arcade ideas that became universal. Super Nintendo and Game Boy releases are much later ports.
breath-of-fire: Capcom's Breath of Fire (1993) is the first RPG in that line, a Super Famicom quest whose hero can take dragon form. A Game Boy Advance reissue is how many English-speaking players later met it.
shin-megami-tensei: Atlus's Shin Megami Tensei is the 1992 Super Famicom RPG of a demon-haunted Tokyo, descended from the Megami Tensei books and Famicom games. Alignment choices shape a bleak modern apocalypse.
pitfall-the-mayan-adventure: Activision's Pitfall: The Mayan Adventure is the 16-bit sequel to David Crane's Atari 2600 Pitfall, using pre-rendered jungle animation. It debuted on Genesis and Super Nintendo in the mid-1990s, not on the 2600.
dragon-quest-v: Enix's DRAGON QUEST V, a 1992 Super Famicom RPG, is famous for marriage, a playable generation, and recruiting monsters. It had no official English release until the Nintendo DS remake.
romancing-saga-3: Square's Romancing SaGa 3 is Akitoshi Kawazu's 1995 Super Famicom RPG, the last of the Romancing SaGa trilogy on that console. Like its predecessors, it waited many years for an official English edition.
tales-of-phantasia: Namco and Wolf Team's Tales of Phantasia is the 1995 Super Famicom game that started the Tales series. Real-time battles and a short voice track were notable on that hardware.
syndicate-1993: Bullfrog's Syndicate (1993) puts you in charge of a four-agent team moving through isometric cities, researching gear as you go. Corporate conquest of the world map is the computer original's signature.
micro-machines-2-turbo-tournament-2: Codemasters' Micro Machines 2: Turbo Tournament continues the toy-car races in 1994, and the Genesis J-Cart lets four people play without an extra adapter. The Super Nintendo version is a separate port of that sequel.
kirbys-dream-land-3-1997: HAL's Kirby's Dream Land 3 (1997) is the Super Nintendo Kirby game with animal friends and a soft pastel look. It is the last Kirby released for that console generation.
blackthorne: Blizzard's Blackthorne, from 1994, is a cinematic platformer also known as Blackhawk, shotgun and long cape included. It launched on the Super Nintendo before later machines, including a Game Boy Advance port.
primal-rage: Atari Games' Primal Rage is a 1995 arcade fighter of stop-motion dinosaurs and giant apes. Home ports, the Super Nintendo one included, carry that prehistoric roster.
tom-jerry: The Super Nintendo Tom & Jerry is a 1993 cartoon platformer, a different production from the NES game subtitled The Ultimate Game of Cat and Mouse. The chase itself is the whole license.
kirbys-dream-course-1994: HAL's Kirby's Dream Course (1994) plays like miniature golf, knocking Kirby into enemies to lower the stroke count. Japan first called the Super Nintendo game Kirby Bowl.
king-of-the-monsters: SNK's KING OF THE MONSTERS is a 1991 Neo Geo grappling game between giant kaiju in cities you can smash. The Super Nintendo version ports that monster-versus-monster coin-op.
demons-crest: Capcom's Demon's Crest (1994) stars the gargoyle Firebrand in a Super Nintendo action game spun out of Gargoyle's Quest. Elemental crests change how he crosses the gothic stages.
grand-theft-auto-1998: DMA Design's Grand Theft Auto, from 1997, is the open-city crime game that started on PC. The Game Boy Color cartridge is a later, much smaller adaptation, not those original cities.
harry-potter-and-the-philosophers-stone: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone is the US title for several different 2001 licenses of the first book and film. Game Boy Color, Game Boy Advance, and home-console editions were made separately and do not play the same.
